presented_options.A: parsing is done lazily inside each handler on a per-need basis; there is no central parser module
presented_options.B: it is a hand-written parser module that reads bytes directly and that no other layer reaches into — routers and middleware consume typed Request / Response values only
presented_options.C: requests are proxied to a trusted upstream server and the parsed form is ingested; the framework itself doesn't parse HTTP
presented_options.D: it is a thin wrapper around a third-party HTTP library (hyper/httparse) configured for strict mode

answers.rationale: Hand-written byte-level parser; no hyper/httparse dependency in Cargo.toml; routers/middleware consume Request/Response.

presented_options.A: it hashes the full path and looks the handler up in a HashMap<(Method, String), Handler>
presented_options.B: it compiles all registered paths into a single regex at startup and runs captures on each request
presented_options.C: it does a linear scan over a Vec<(Method, String, Handler)> and falls back to a 404 on the first non-match
presented_options.D: it walks a trie whose node kinds are literal / parameter / wildcard; match is O(path-length) and allocates only the parameter map

answers.rationale: Router uses a trie of Literal/Param/Wildcard nodes with a HashMap<method,handler> per node.

presented_options.A: an OPTIONS request on a defined route returns an Allow header listing the methods registered for that path
presented_options.B: registering GET /users automatically registers POST /users with the same handler for convenience
presented_options.C: a HEAD request reuses the GET handler and omits the body from the response
presented_options.D: path parameters (e.g. /users/:id) are captured and made available to the handler through a typed params map

answers.rationale: Routes are registered per (method, path); GET registration does not implicitly register POST.

presented_options.A: each middleware is a closure stored in a Vec; the chain is executed by a fold over that Vec each request
presented_options.B: each middleware implements a single object-safe trait; the chain is a list of trait objects whose registration order drives outer-to-inner call order
presented_options.C: middlewares are chosen per request by a proc-macro that expanded at compile time to a different fn for each route
presented_options.D: middlewares are composed via tower::Layer and tower::Service; nanoweb re-exports the tower types

answers.rationale: Object-safe async trait; Vec<Arc<dyn Middleware>>; Next walks list in registration order so first added is outermost.

presented_options.A: TLS is a required dependency; the crate does not compile without rustls
presented_options.B: TLS is a runtime decision based on the NANOWEB_TLS env var; both code paths are always compiled
presented_options.C: TLS lives in a separate sibling crate nanoweb-tls that the main crate re-exports
presented_options.D: TLS is gated by a Cargo feature (tls) that is enabled by default; with the feature off the crate still builds and the --tls-cert flag emits a clear error

answers.rationale: Cargo feature `tls` is in default features; rustls deps are optional; tls module and error variant are cfg-gated.

presented_options.A: it drains the TCP buffers but keeps the process alive so a supervisor can signal readiness again
presented_options.B: it exits immediately; in-flight connections are dropped mid-response
presented_options.C: it stops accepting new connections, lets in-flight requests complete up to a bounded graceful_timeout_s, then exits 0
presented_options.D: it hot-reloads the config without exiting; shutdown requires SIGQUIT

answers.rationale: On signal, accept loop breaks, then waits up to graceful_timeout_s for in-flight permits before exiting.

presented_options.A: it emits OpenTelemetry OTLP over gRPC to a collector configured via env var
presented_options.B: it mounts a Prometheus text-exposition endpoint at a configurable path with per-method/status/route counters and a request-duration histogram
presented_options.C: it writes one statsd UDP packet per request to localhost:8125
presented_options.D: it logs one structured JSON line per request; aggregation happens downstream

answers.rationale: Prometheus text exposition with http_requests_total counter and http_request_duration_seconds histogram, mounted at metrics_path.

presented_options.A: it correlates requests only within a session cookie; there is no per-request id
presented_options.B: it generates a fresh id per request, attaches it to the structured log context for that request, and mirrors it to the response as X-Request-Id
presented_options.C: it passes an inbound X-Correlation-Id through unchanged and does nothing if the header is absent
presented_options.D: it uses the TCP connection's 4-tuple as an implicit id; no HTTP header is set

answers.rationale: No request-id generation, no X-Request-Id/X-Correlation-Id handling; only peer_addr is logged in errors — no HTTP correlation header is set.

presented_options.A: inside a single config module that loads TOML, applies CLI overrides, and yields one Config struct that all other modules consume
presented_options.B: inside clap's derive macros via #[arg(default_value_from_fn)] hooks that reach into the TOML at parse time
presented_options.C: scattered across each consuming module — wherever a value is read, the module checks CLI then TOML
presented_options.D: inside main as a long if-else chain immediately before tokio::main boots the server

answers.rationale: config module owns Config + ConfigOverrides + apply_overrides; main loads TOML, passes CLI overrides, gets one Config used everywhere.

presented_options.A: a minimal mustache-style renderer with variable interpolation ({{name}}), sections ({{#list}}{{/list}}), and inverted sections ({{^absent}}{{/absent}})
presented_options.B: there is no template engine; handlers build HTML by hand
presented_options.C: a compile-time HTML macro (like maud) that produces typed HTML fragments
presented_options.D: a full Jinja2-compatible engine with filters, macros, template inheritance, and sandboxed eval

answers.rationale: Mustache-style: {{name}} interpolation, {{#list}}{{/list}} sections, {{^absent}}{{/absent}} inverted sections per README and template module.

presented_options.A: logger, gzip, rate limit, CORS, CSRF, basic auth — exactly the six types registered in the default middleware chain
presented_options.B: logger, gzip, sliding-window rate limit per API key, CORS, OAuth2 bearer guard
presented_options.C: logger, gzip, token-bucket rate limit per client IP, CORS, double-submit-cookie CSRF, basic auth
presented_options.D: logger as the outermost middleware, with basic auth among the inner middlewares

answers.rationale: Shipped middleware are logging, gzip, rate_limiting, cors, csrf, basic_auth. No OAuth2 bearer guard exists, so option B is inconsistent.

presented_options.A: errors are stringly typed: Result<T, String> end to end
presented_options.B: errors are conveyed by panicking on the fallible path and recovering via catch_unwind at the accept loop
presented_options.C: a single NanowebError enum is the return type of top-level fallible entry points; submodule errors convert at their public boundary
presented_options.D: each submodule exposes its own error type; the server returns Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> and callers downcast

answers.rationale: Single NanowebError enum with submodule-specific variants is the public Result error type throughout the crate.

presented_options.A: waits indefinitely until every in-flight request completes, then exits with code 0
presented_options.B: waits up to ~30 seconds, then exits with code 0; the two long-running handlers are abandoned mid-response
presented_options.C: aborts immediately on SIGTERM, replying 503 to all in-flight connections, then exits non-zero
presented_options.D: exits with code 1 because at least one request was still in flight when the timeout elapsed

answers.rationale: Default graceful_timeout_s=30; the wait is wrapped in tokio::time::timeout, so after ~30s the server exits Ok regardless of remaining handlers.

presented_options.A: the parser imports its own internal helper submodules (e.g. chunked-body decoder, header folding) but nothing from outside `http::`
presented_options.B: the parser imports the router module (e.g. trie node types or route-match results)
presented_options.C: the parser imports byte-handling helpers (std::str, the `bytes` crate, or equivalent) and the crate's `error` module
presented_options.D: the parser imports HTTP shape types (Method, Header, Version) from a sibling `http::types` (or equivalent) module

answers.rationale: Parser only imports http::types and std::collections; it does not import the router module.

presented_options.A: starts a plain HTTP listener on 8443 and ignores the TLS flags with a warning on stderr
presented_options.B: prints a clear error explaining TLS support was not compiled in (the `tls` feature is off) and exits non-zero without binding the port
presented_options.C: panics on the unrecognised flag — the TLS-related CLI flags only exist when the feature is on
presented_options.D: starts an HTTPS listener using a self-signed cert generated at startup; the user-supplied cert files are ignored

answers.rationale: CLI flags are not feature-gated and the server only uses TcpListener — tls_cert/tls_key are stored on Config but never consumed, so a plain HTTP listener binds and TLS flags are effectively ignored.
